editor_spans.body: Burnham's speech in Motherwell tells a single story about Ravenscraig, Leigh and Scottish centralisation: distant decision-makers abandoned places, and the fix is to push power down. The history he leaves out complicates his diagnosis. Ravenscraig closed in 1992. The owner was British Steel, privatised in 1988, so the decision was a corporate one made under a Westminster government that had already given up on industrial strategy. In 1992 no level of local government could have stopped it. That did not change when the Scottish Parliament arrived. Pushing power down to regions does nothing about decisions made in boardrooms, and that is how the next Ravenscraig would most likely happen. Grangemouth, which he mentions himself, is the current example.

The more pointed omission concerns who centralised Scotland. In 1996, three years before Holyrood existed, Westminster abolished Strathclyde Regional Council and the other Scottish regions. Strathclyde covered Motherwell, Glasgow and Inverclyde and was exactly the kind of strong regional body Burnham now wants to build. Holyrood then inherited 32 unitary councils with no regional tier above them. Later Scottish governments made things worse with years of council tax freezes and ring-fenced funding. So when he calls Scotland 'one of the most centralised nations in Europe', he is describing a structure that Westminster and Holyrood built between them. Blaming it on Edinburgh alone, as the Number 10 briefing did, is selective history. The City Region Deals he praises were a partial attempt to rebuild the regional level that 1996 took away.

The concrete part of the offer is DWP devolution, and it shows how the offer is built. Holyrood already has some employability powers, and Burnham is offering a localised employment-support model 'shaped by Holyrood'. But he then says it 'has to be based on the Easterhouse principle' and must 'go right down'. Westminster would hand over a power and also set how far down Holyrood has to pass it on. That fits what I argued before: the offer is designed so that Westminster wins whether Edinburgh accepts or refuses. What will show whether it is real is whether the money for it gets close to what Greater Manchester's devolution deals came with. Without that money, Holyrood would get a target to meet but not the means to meet it.
